description: Explorers of Infinity is an interdisciplinary research team connecting India and Poland, driven by curiosity about mathematics, theoretical physics, cosmology, and the Universe. Our expertise spans astrophysics, computational modelling, engineering, and AI. For NASA's Planet X and SPHEREx challenge, we aim to develop an interactive infrared sky explorer using real astronomical observations, rigorous scientific analysis, and data visualization to investigate the changing Universe.
summary:
SPHEREx Observation Lab is a public web application that turns authentic NASA SPHEREx infrared observations into an accessible, time-domain sky explorer. It addresses the Planet X and SPHEREx challenge by helping users inspect sky positions, compare repeated observations and watch how astronomical fields change over time.

Our published Streamlit prototype includes chronological playback, blink and side-by-side views, wavelength and detector metadata, celestial-coordinate handling, quality-mask overlays, downloadable evidence and guided examples involving nearby stars and brown dwarfs. A reproducible offline dataset of 39 real SPHEREx cutouts and their calibration/PSF products keeps the demonstration usable even when live archive requests fail.

We use calibrated SPHEREx data from NASA/IPAC IRSA, supported by Astropy and reference catalogues. We checked representative FITS images, WCS coordinates, pixel values and official photometry. The application distinguishes visual differences from validated physical detections: it does not claim to have discovered Planet X or proven source variability. Our goal is credible, approachable exploration of the changing infrared sky.
details:
SPHEREx Observation Lab

The Problem and Our Solution

NASA's SPHEREx mission observes the infrared sky across 102 spectral bands, enabling astronomers to investigate celestial objects and how they change with time. However, working directly with astronomical FITS images, detector metadata, sky-coordinate transformations and multi-epoch observations can be challenging for students, educators and the public.

Our solution is SPHEREx Observation Lab, an interactive, publicly accessible web application that allows users to explore genuine NASA SPHEREx observations through chronological image sequences and scientific visualization tools.

The goal is to make changes in the infrared sky easier to investigate without requiring specialist astronomy software.

How Our Application Works

The application uses authentic SPHEREx Level-2 observations distributed through NASA/IPAC's Infrared Science Archive (IRSA).

Users can inspect astronomical fields through an interactive browser interface, compare repeated observations and examine the scientific metadata associated with each image.

The published application provides:

  • Chronological image sequences, playback and frame stepping.
  • Side-by-side and blink comparisons between observation epochs.
  • Celestial-coordinate handling using astronomical World Coordinate Systems.
  • Detector, wavelength and observation-date information.
  • Image-quality masks and scientific diagnostic information.
  • Reference catalogue information, including Gaia and WISE where supported.
  • Guided exploration of astronomical targets such as Epsilon Indi B, Barnard's Star and WISE 0855.
  • Downloadable metadata and reproducibility information.

The application includes 39 authentic SPHEREx science-image cutouts and associated calibration and effective point-spread-function products. This packaged dataset supports reliable demonstrations even when the live NASA archive is temporarily unavailable.

The application also includes bounded live archive-access functionality, subject to network and service availability.

Scientific and Technical Implementation

The platform is developed using Python and Streamlit, with scientific computations and image processing supported by Astropy, NumPy and related open-source scientific libraries.

FITS files preserve the original astronomical science measurements, while WCS transformations connect celestial coordinates with detector pixels.

Image metadata, quality flags, uncertainty information and observational provenance are retained wherever applicable.

We deliberately distinguish raw detector-pixel measurements, displayed images and calibrated astrophysical source-flux measurements.

Validation and Scientific Accuracy

Our team manually inspected real SPHEREx FITS observations and verified image dimensions, pixel values, coordinate transformations, wavelength metadata, variance arrays and quality flags.

For the Epsilon Indi B demonstration, we compared observations from October 2025 and September 2026 and examined selected results against official SPHEREx photometry.

The resulting photometric comparison was statistically inconclusive. We therefore do not claim a new detection, confirmed source variability or the discovery of Planet X.

The published application was also tested through automated software checks and independent browser verification.

Challenges and Lessons Learned

Important challenges included obtaining and validating authentic observations, handling archive-service failures, preserving astronomical coordinates, understanding instrumental resolution, accounting for different wavelength bands and avoiding misleading interpretations of image differences.

Our development process incorporated corrections to earlier scientific assumptions, software failures and interpretation errors.

We also developed safeguards to distinguish missing observations from genuine astronomical nondetections.

Impact and Creativity

SPHEREx Observation Lab combines an accessible educational interface with real scientific data, reproducible processing and transparent measurement limitations.

It enables students, astronomy enthusiasts and researchers to examine the changing infrared sky using authentic mission observations.

Our long-term vision is to extend the platform with wider multi-epoch coverage, robust image alignment, scientifically validated stacking and more advanced moving-object investigations.

These future developments are distinguished from the capabilities already implemented in the published application.
